Meaning: The driver detected a controller error on the device during a retried I/O operation.
NextStep: Back up data immediately and check the drive's SMART status (Storage tab); consider replacing the drive if this recurs.

Meaning: The driver detected a controller error on the device.
NextStep: Check SMART status and replace the drive/cable if this recurs.

Meaning: The device is not ready for access yet - Windows tried to use the drive before it was ready.
NextStep: Usually harmless for external/USB drives; if it recurs on an internal fixed drive, check SMART status.

Meaning: The file system structure on the volume is corrupt and unusable.
NextStep: Run chkdsk /f on the affected volume as soon as possible.

Meaning: The volume's dirty bit is set - NTFS believes the file system needs a consistency check.
NextStep: Run chkdsk on the volume at next reboot, or from an elevated prompt.

Meaning: The default transaction resource manager on the volume encountered a non-retryable error and could not start.
NextStep: Run chkdsk on the affected volume.

Meaning: The AHCI storage driver reset a device because it did not respond in time.
NextStep: Check SMART status and cable seating; treat repeated resets as an early failure warning.

Meaning: The NVMe storage driver reset a device because it did not respond in time.
NextStep: Check SMART/NVMe health and update the SSD firmware if available.

Meaning: A fatal hardware error was corrected by the hardware/firmware (a corrected machine-check event).
NextStep: Occasional isolated events are common; frequent recurrence warrants memory/CPU stress testing.

Meaning: An uncorrected hardware error occurred (machine-check exception) - often the cause of an unexpected reboot/BSOD.
NextStep: Run memory diagnostics (Windows Memory Diagnostic / MemTest86), reset any overclock, and check the Stability tab's Minidumps for a correlated crash.

Meaning: A general WHEA hardware error record was logged.
LikelyCauses: Hardware instability of some kind - CPU, memory, PCIe device, or firmware
NextStep: Check the event detail for the specific error source; correlate with WHEA 17/18 for corrected vs. uncorrected severity.

Meaning: A service terminated unexpectedly and, per its recovery settings, will be restarted.
NextStep: Check the service's own logs and the Application log around this time for the underlying crash; restart the service from the Services tab if it hasn't already recovered.

Meaning: A service did not respond to the start or control request in time (a hang).
NextStep: Try restarting the service; if it consistently times out, check its dependencies and startup type.

Meaning: A service failed to start due to an error.
NextStep: Check the specific error code in the event detail and the service's configured logon account and dependencies.

Meaning: One or more boot-start or system-start drivers failed to load.
LikelyCauses: Driver disabled by policy or a Safe Mode boot flag
NextStep: Check Device Manager for the affected driver and reinstall/update it.

Meaning: A service terminated with a specific (non-zero) service-specific error code.
LikelyCauses: The service's own internal failure - the specific code is in the event detail
NextStep: Look up the service-specific error code for that particular service; it's often documented per-product.

Meaning: An application (identified by its CLSID/APPID) was denied the DCOM permissions it requested, so Windows fell back to default permissions.
LikelyCauses: A built-in Windows component or app requesting permissions it doesn't strictly need
Extremely common and largely cosmetic on modern Windows
NextStep: Usually safe to ignore; only worth acting on if a specific app is visibly failing at the same time this event appears.

Meaning: DCOM was unable to communicate with the computer, or a required service failed to launch on demand.
LikelyCauses: A DCOM server failed to start
NextStep: If a specific feature is failing, check whether the referenced service/component is installed and its startup type.

Meaning: The server (identified by CLSID) did not register with DCOM within the required timeout.
LikelyCauses: Server process slow to start or crashed on launch
NextStep: Usually transient; investigate only if a specific feature relying on that CLSID is broken.

Meaning: The performance counters for a specific service/driver are corrupt - the Open/Collect/Close DLL functions for that counter set failed.
LikelyCauses: A buggy or mismatched counter DLL after an update
NextStep: Rebuild performance counters (lodctr /R from an elevated prompt) if any perf-counter-based monitoring for that provider is misbehaving.

Meaning: The performance counter registry data for a service is inconsistent or corrupt.
LikelyCauses: Same root cause family as Perflib 1008
NextStep: Rebuild performance counters (lodctr /R) if this correlates with monitoring tools misbehaving.

Meaning: The system rebooted without cleanly shutting down first - the classic 'this was a real crash' signal that Reliability Monitor itself keys on.
NextStep: Check the Stability tab's Minidumps and bugcheck code; if it recurs, suspect a driver, PSU, or overheating.

Meaning: Disk resource exhaustion was detected - a process or the system is generating I/O faster than the disk can absorb it, risking system unresponsiveness.
LikelyCauses: A runaway process doing heavy disk I/O
Insufficient free disk space causing thrashing
NextStep: Check the Processes tab for a disk-heavy process, and confirm the system drive isn't nearly full or failing.

Meaning: A shadow copy (Volume Shadow Copy / System Restore point) was deleted, usually because the storage allocated for shadow copies filled up.
LikelyCauses: Large amount of disk churn shrinking available shadow storage
NextStep: Increase shadow storage allocation (vssadmin resize shadowstorage) if System Restore/previous versions are needed further back.

Meaning: The shadow copies of a volume were aborted because the volume was force-dismounted.
LikelyCauses: A backup or maintenance tool force-dismounted the volume mid-operation
A removable drive pulled during a VSS operation
NextStep: Usually a one-off tied to a specific backup/maintenance operation; investigate only if backups are failing.

Meaning: An ESE (Extensible Storage Engine) database failed to initialize due to a JET error.
LikelyCauses: Corrupt Windows Search or Windows Update ESE-backed database
Disk error while the database was open
Unclean shutdown while the database was mid-write
NextStep: For Windows Search, rebuild the search index (Indexing Options > Advanced > Rebuild); for Windows Update's datastore, consider resetting the Windows Update components.

Meaning: An ESE database was found in an inconsistent state (dirty shutdown) and recovery is required.
LikelyCauses: Unclean shutdown while the database was open
NextStep: The database engine usually self-repairs on next open; if the affected app/service keeps failing, rebuild its database (e.g. the Windows Search index).

Meaning: An ESE database exceeded its configured maximum size.
LikelyCauses: A monitored/logged dataset has grown beyond the database's configured cap
NextStep: Identify which ESE-backed component this is (often Windows Search or a mail store) and clear/rebuild or resize it.

Meaning: A fatal TLS/SSL alert was received during a secure connection handshake.
LikelyCauses: Protocol/cipher mismatch with the remote server
NextStep: Check which application/connection triggered this and verify its certificate chain and supported TLS versions.

Meaning: A fatal alert was generated and sent to the remote endpoint, closing the connection - the local-side counterpart to event 36887.
LikelyCauses: Same TLS/certificate/protocol mismatch causes as event 36887
NextStep: Same as event 36887 - check certificate and TLS version compatibility for the affected connection.

Meaning: An unrecoverable error occurred while creating a TLS/SSL context, and the connection was terminated.
NextStep: Check the affected service's certificate binding and that its account has access to its private key.

Meaning: A TLS fatal alert was generated, most commonly because the client and server share no compatible TLS/cipher configuration.
LikelyCauses: Legacy TLS 1.0/1.1 disabled on one side
NextStep: Verify the TLS version/cipher configuration on both endpoints matches.

Meaning: Group Policy processing failed because a domain controller could not be reached (or this PC simply isn't domain-joined).
LikelyCauses: Not domain-joined - a home/workgroup PC; this is expected and harmless
VPN not connected on a domain-joined laptop
DNS/network issue reaching a real domain controller
NextStep: Expected and safe to ignore on a non-domain-joined PC; on a domain-joined machine, check network/VPN connectivity to a domain controller.

Meaning: Windows failed to apply one or more Group Policy settings because it could not read the policy data.
NextStep: On a domain-joined PC, run gpupdate /force and check connectivity to a domain controller; not applicable to a non-domain PC.

Meaning: Group Policy failed to read the gpt.ini file for a policy object, most often a network/DFS access problem.
LikelyCauses: SYSVOL/DFS replication issue on the domain controller
NextStep: Domain-only issue; check SYSVOL access and DNS resolution to the domain controller.

Meaning: The time service (w32time) could not find a usable time source and stopped advertising as a reliable time source.
NextStep: Check network connectivity and the configured time source (w32tm /query /status).

Meaning: The time service has lost contact with its configured time source(s) for an extended period.
NextStep: Verify NTP (UDP 123) isn't blocked and the configured time server is reachable.

Meaning: The system clock was found to be inaccurate and was corrected by more than the configured tolerance in one jump.
LikelyCauses: Clock drift from an extended period offline
NextStep: A one-off is harmless; if it recurs on every boot, the CMOS/RTC battery may need replacing.

Meaning: The time provider is receiving invalid time data from its source and cannot use it.
NextStep: Check the configured NTP server address; the default time.windows.com is usually reliable.

Meaning: TCP/IP failed to establish an outgoing connection because the local dynamic port range was exhausted or a security limit was hit.
LikelyCauses: A very large number of concurrent outbound connections (a runaway app, or a port-exhausting bug)
Ports held in TIME_WAIT under heavy churn
NextStep: Identify which process is opening excessive connections (Network tab's connection list) and restart/fix it.

Meaning: TCP/IP detected a potential port-exhaustion problem in advance - fewer than a low-watermark of local ports remained available.
LikelyCauses: Same causes as event 4227 - a process opening far more outbound connections than normal
NextStep: Same as event 4227 - find and fix the process opening excessive outbound connections.

Meaning: TCP/IP could not renew or bind an IP address configuration for a network adapter.
NextStep: Check DHCP connectivity, or try releasing/renewing the adapter's IP configuration.

Meaning: An ETW trace session failed to start, usually because it raced with another component starting the same session at boot.
LikelyCauses: Boot-time session-start ordering race - benign in the vast majority of cases
NextStep: Usually safe to ignore unless a specific diagnostic/logging tool is visibly missing data.

Meaning: An ETW trace session could not be stopped cleanly, typically during the same kind of startup/shutdown race as event 2.
LikelyCauses: Session lifecycle race - benign in the vast majority of cases
NextStep: Usually safe to ignore.

Meaning: The previous system shutdown was unexpected - the legacy plain-text equivalent of Kernel-Power event 41.
NextStep: Same follow-up as Kernel-Power 41 - check the Stability tab's Minidumps and bugcheck code.

Meaning: An application crashed - the generic 'faulting application' entry Windows Error Reporting logs for any unhandled application exception.
LikelyCauses: A bug in the faulting module named in the event
A corrupted install of that application
An incompatible plugin/add-in loaded into the app
NextStep: Check the Stability tab's 'Crashes by faulting module' grouping - a module that recurs across multiple crashes is the actual culprit to reinstall/update.

Meaning: Windows Error Reporting's summary of the most recent Blue Screen (bugcheck), logged after the reboot that followed it.
LikelyCauses: Same causes as any BSOD - driver fault, hardware fault, or a kernel-level software bug
NextStep: Check the Stability tab's Minidumps for the specific bugcheck code and correlate with any driver update around that time.

Meaning: Windows detected the system was critically low on memory (commit/available memory) and is warning before things start failing.
LikelyCauses: Too many applications open for installed RAM
NextStep: Check the Processes tab for the highest memory consumer; consider adding RAM or increasing the page file.

Meaning: Windows automatically took action (e.g. terminated a process) to recover from a critically-low-memory condition.
LikelyCauses: Same as event 2004 - a memory-leaking or oversized workload that pushed the system over the edge
NextStep: Identify which process was terminated in the event detail and investigate its memory usage.
